entry.title: One Click to a Clean Employee Record: Print and Export People Profile to PDF in 2H 2026
entry.content:
The screenshot workaround ends

From 13 November 2026, anyone who can view a latest People Profile can export it to a clean, dated PDF. It is switched on automatically and has no permission of its own. That makes it both a big productivity win and a governance item HR must review before go-live.

Today, when a talent committee, an auditor or an executive needs an employee summary, HR improvises. Someone takes screenshots of profile cards, pastes them into a slide or Word file, and hopes nothing changed since. The output is inconsistent, undated and hard to trust.

The new Print Profile action replaces that with a standard, as-of-dated document. The release note tags it "Info only". In my view, that undersells it: a feature that lets data leave the system deserves a deliberate decision.

What SAP shipped in 2H 2026

Print Profile sits in the Actions menu of the latest People Profile and exports Spotlight and Full Profile data to PDF. You choose the whole profile or specific categories and cards, then preview and remove individual cards before exporting.

 

What the PDF contains

Details

Timestamp

Print time, in the logged-in user's locale

As-of date

Matches the date selected on the Full Profile, so effective-dated data reflects that date

Header data

Everything visible in the Full Profile header and Profile Preview, except self-descriptions and matrix managers

Cards

Full details page where one exists, otherwise the summary card; original order kept, Documents always last

Empty fields

Always included

Status indicators

Pending Workflow and future-change notices appear; so do error messages

Attachments

Shown as file names only

Removed

Action buttons and card help

File name

[DisplayName]Profile[Date].pdf

Why it matters for HR

The as-of date is what makes this more than a print button. Every PDF states exactly which date the effective-dated data reflects, so the document can stand as a record. Four HR situations benefit right away.

Talent and succession reviews. Committees often include leaders who rarely log in. HR can prepare a consistent pack of candidate profiles, limited to the relevant categories, in minutes.

Audits and compliance checks. An auditor asks what an employee's job and contract data looked like on a given date. Set the Full Profile date, export, and the PDF carries both the as-of date and the print timestamp.

Employee relations and legal matters. Case files need a dated snapshot of the record at a point in time. A system-generated PDF is cleaner evidence than a screenshot.

Transfers, mergers and offboarding. When a record must move to another entity, or be retained for a period, HR has a standard format instead of ad-hoc extracts.

SAP positions it for talent managers, recruiters, compliance officers and executives who need profile data without direct system access. That last phrase is exactly why governance matters.

Governance: the part not to skip

Print appears for every user who can access the latest People Profile and view the data, with no separate permission to grant or withhold. In practice, your view permissions now also decide who can export profiles to a portable file.

SAP has built in sensible protections:

  • Data the user has no permission for is hidden in the PDF, as on screen.
  • Fields masked in the data model stay masked; unmasking in print is not supported.
  • The annualized salary chart is left out, and the amount field is always masked.

What the system cannot control is what happens to the file afterwards. A PDF can be emailed, saved to a personal drive or printed and left on a desk. For HR, that raises questions worth answering before 13 November:

  • Are our view permissions still right now that viewing also means exporting? Pay special attention to managers, matrix roles and broad "view all" HR groups.
  • Which categories hold sensitive data, such as dependents, national IDs, payment details or health-related leave, and are they masked or restricted?
  • Does our data retention and acceptable-use policy cover exported employee records?
  • Do works councils or privacy officers in any country need to be informed?

The annualized salary exclusion shows SAP thought about pay sensitivity. Your own sensitive custom fields need the same thought from you.

Rollout steps, watch-outs and tests

Because it switches on by itself, the work is a pre-release review rather than a configuration task. The steps and test ideas below are my suggestions.

  1. Review view permissions in preview. Treat "can view" as "can export" and adjust roles that are broader than they need to be.
  2. Check masking on sensitive fields. Confirm which fields are masked in the data model, because masking carries into the PDF.
  3. Brief privacy and legal. Agree how exported profiles may be stored, shared and deleted.
  4. Communicate to users. Tell HR, managers and executives what the feature is for, and what it is not for.
  5. Build use-case templates. For talent reviews, define which categories to include so packs look the same every time.

 

Test

What to check

Manager vs HR admin export of the same employee

Each PDF shows only what that role can see on screen

Masked custom field

Stays masked in the PDF

Compensation category

Salary chart absent, amount masked

Past as-of date on Full Profile

PDF data and as-of date match that date

Record with a pending workflow

Pending notice appears, so readers know data may change

Documents category

Prints last, with attachment file names only

Long profile in different browsers

Layout and page breaks are readable

Closing thought

Print Profile solves a real, everyday HR problem: getting a trustworthy, dated employee record to people who are not in the system. Its as-of date and built-in masking make it far better than any screenshot.

But it arrives switched on, with no permission of its own. The HR teams that get the most from it will be the ones who spend an hour in preview checking who can view what. Do that, and you gain a clean record in one click without opening a new data risk.

Sources

  • SAP SuccessFactors What's New, 2H 2026 Platform release notes: "Print and Export People Profile to PDF" (ECT-268339, valid as of 13 November 2026).
  • SAP Help: Configuring the Latest People Profile (Printing People Profile)

entry.title: Understanding the changes to Rehires in H2 2026 Onboarding release.
entry.content:
In the H2 release for Onboarding there are some significant changes to how the rehire process works.  There is a very detailed blog here.  However, we have tried to distil this even further for users to understand easily.

Before we start it is interesting to confirm how rehires work in Employee Central. 

In Employee Central if you have a Contingent Worker (CW) whose end date has passed, you can’t rehire onto that record as an employee or a CW.  You need a ‘Rehire on a New Employment’. 

You can extend a contingent worker if the end date has not passed but once it is passed you can’t change the end date you need to do a rehire.

Scenario A – Rehiring an inactive contingent worker as an employee

Let’s assume we you have a contingent worker whose work order end date has passed and they are inactive.  If they were returning via onboarding as an employee, the system (prior to this release) would allow you to ‘Rehire on the Old Employment’ onto the inactive CW record.  This action would throw errors in Employee Central as it is not allowed.  As a result, in this release you can no longer do this.  The system will force you to rehire on a new employment as this is how it works in Employee Central.

 

Scenario B – Rehiring an inactive contingent worker as an employee

Let’s assume we you have a contingent worker whose work order end date has passed and they have a separate inactive employee record i.e. they have two inactive records.  If they were returning via onboarding as an employee, the system will allow you to rehire on the old employee record (subject to RBP) on the employee record or Rehire on a New Employment. It won’t allow you to rehire on the old employment on the CW worker record as described in Scenario A.

 

Scenario C – Rehiring an active contingent worker as an employee with a future date termination

If you had a contingent worker whose work order end date is in the future.  You can now rehire as an employee with a new employment after the future dated termination.

 Additional Comments

  1. If you have an employee who has a future date termination and you want to rehire them via onboarding, the system only supports Rehire on New Employment and not Rehire on Old Employment.  This has not changed in this release. 
  2.  
  3. When you perform the rehire checks.  In the release product talks about adding in a ‘surface layers’, these are effectively new pop up screens to help you process the rehire.  For rehire on old employment you can add in the correct event reason without having to complete the whole process.

If there are any data errors when you rehire you will be redirected to adjust the data errors, this is available for rehire on old and new employments

There is another feature ‘Rehire on New Employment with Future Termination’ and I will be writing a separate article about this.  Once this is published, I will link it here.

Hopefully this blog has summarized the main points from the H2 2026 Onboarding release relating to rehires.

entry.title: SAP SuccessFactors 2H 2026 Release: RBPs are Changing, Here’s What to Check Before November 13, 2026
entry.content:
Why this release matters

 

The 2H 2026 release includes six changes to Role-Based Permissions (RBP) and the areas around it. They cover who can act as a proxy, which MDF objects are secured by default, how Learning administrators are assigned, how RBP changes are audited, what Performance Management data shows up in Story reports, and what the RBP REST APIs return.

SAP rates two of them Major (proxy and Learning). All six are valid as of 13 November 2026. Five switch on automatically, and only the Story permission is customer-configured.

 

Change

Reference

Type

Major / Minor

Enablement

Module-level proxy access control

PLA-57182

Changed

Major

Automatically on

More MDF objects secured by default

ECT-257018

Changed

Minor

Automatically on

Learning admin roles assigned through RBP

PLA-57203

Changed

Major

Automatically on

RBP change audit reports in two versions (V2)

PLA-56544

Changed

Minor

Automatically on

Hide Story report data for forms never in Inbox

PMU-27006

New

Minor

Customer configured

RBP REST API enhancements

PLA-58003

Changed

Minor

Automatically on

 

Facts in this post come from SAP’s 2H 2026 release notes (latest revision 2 October 2026). Anything labelled Suggested is my recommendation, not SAP’s.

 

1. Proxy: creating proxies and acting as a proxy are now separate permissions

Before: Holding Proxy Management did two jobs. It gave access to the Proxy Management UI to create proxy assignments for the target population. It also let the holder act on behalf of their entire target population for all proxy modules, without an explicit 1:1 proxy assignment. There was no option to restrict proxy access to specific modules in RBP.

Now: The two jobs are separate permissions.

 

Permission

What it does now

Proxy Management

Gives access to the Proxy Management UI to create assignments for the target population.

Proxy Rights (under General User Permission)

Lets administrators act on behalf of their target population for the selected proxy modules. Also used to create group-to-group proxy assignments.

 

When you define a Proxy Rights permission role in Admin Center > Manage Permission Roles, you set:

  • Access Population: the users who will act as proxy.
  • Target Population: the users the access population can proxy into.
  • Proxy Modules: all modules or a selected subset, shown in a parent-child hierarchy. Selecting a child module automatically includes its parent.

What happens at release: To avoid disruption, anyone holding Proxy Management at release is automatically granted Proxy Rights with all modules selected. No manual migration step is required. To narrow a role, open it in Manage Permission Roles and update the proxy module selection under the Proxy Rights settings.

Watch-outs from the release note:

  • Selecting the Reporting proxy module or its sub-modules gives the proxy access to all reports. Selecting Performance Management Forms gives access to all Performance Management forms. For more granular control of reports and forms, use the Proxy Management admin tool.
  • To act as a proxy, a user needs either Proxy Rights or an explicit 1:1 proxy assignment created through the Proxy Management tool. When both apply, the explicit 1:1 assignment takes priority.
  • To open the Proxy Management UI, you need the Proxy Management permission in your role.

Why it matters: SAP’s own summary is that you can now give specific administrators access to the proxy management UI without also granting them proxy access.

Suggested: Because the automatic grant is all modules, list everyone who holds Proxy Management and decide who needs all modules, some modules or no proxy rights.

 

2. More MDF objects are secured by default

Before: For these objects, the Access to non-secured objects permission was necessary to view, create and update records. All users who held it could also add and delete objects.

Now: From 2H 2026, eight MDF objects are delivered as secured by default. SAP states that it is not possible to change this setting:

  • Position
  • Position Type
  • Position Right to Return
  • Position Requisition Mapping
  • Position Job Requisition Processing Request
  • Position Requisition Status
  • Company Structure Definition
  • Company Structure UI Configuration

What happens to your existing roles depends on where you started:

 

Your situation

What happens

You had already secured the object

No change

The object was not secured, and the role does not have Access to non-secured objects

No change

The object was not secured, but the role does have Access to non-secured objects

The system grants the role permissions on the object from the new User > Position Management Object Permissions category

 

Two objects from 1H 2026 were also re-documented in this release “for clarity”. They follow the same three-way logic, but the grants go to different categories:

 

Object

Delivered

Where the system grants permissions

Hire Date Correction

1H 2026

Manage Data category: Object-Level Permissions, View, Edit, Import, Export, View Pending Approvals and Review Pending Approvals. The release note says there are no changes to permissions granted in the “Manager User” category.

Fallback Event Reason Configuration

1H 2026

Administrator > Manage Business Configuration category

 

Why SAP made the change: It is part of a general initiative to make all unsecured MDF objects secure by default, so customers make informed decisions on which target groups they provide appropriate permissions to.

Suggested: List the roles that hold Access to non-secured objects and open each in Manage Permission Roles. Review the permissions the system granted under Position Management Object Permissions, Manage Data and Manage Business Configuration. The old permission allowed adding and deleting, so check what the new grants allow and remove anything the role doesn’t need.

 

3. Learning admin roles can now be assigned through RBP

Learning administrator roles can now be assigned in Admin Center > Manage Permission Roles, in addition to the existing standalone Learning role assignment function. In Step 2 (Add Permissions), roles appear as dynamic child permissions under a new permission, Learning Administrator Role Assignment.

How it works:

  • The child permissions are synced from Learning. When Learning admin roles are added or removed in Learning, the child permissions update after the automatically triggered Refresh RBP Model job completes.
  • After you assign the permission to administrators, a daily job, Sync Learning Admin Role Access to Learning, syncs those administrators to Learning. The job runs in delta mode automatically. If you see data inconsistencies, you can trigger a full sync manually in Scheduled Job Manager.
  • If the admin user doesn’t exist in Learning, they are created automatically during role assignment.
  • Assignment and revocation are reflected in Learning within approximately 15 minutes of the sync job completing. Changes are not immediate.
  • Changes to permission groups, such as adding or removing members, are reflected in Learning after the sync job runs.
  • You don’t need to grant Learning admin roles in both RBP and Learning. Managing them through RBP is sufficient.

Rules in the role editor:

  • Selecting only Learning Admin Access Permission, without a role under Learning Administrator Role Assignment, shows an informational message.
  • Selecting Learning Administrator Role Assignment and at least one role selects Learning Admin Access Permission automatically.
  • Unselecting Learning Admin Access Permission also unselects Learning Administrator Role Assignment and resets the dropdown.
  • Selecting Learning Administrator Role Assignment without choosing a role shows an error asking you to provide values for the highlighted fields.

Prerequisite: Learning must be installed in integrated and sealed mode and run version 2H 2026 or higher. If Learning isn’t integrated, is integrated but not sealed, or runs an earlier version, a warning appears in Manage Permission Roles and Learning administrator roles are not shown or available for assignment. SAP points to KBA 3193649 for sealing your Learning instance.

Person mode: If Learning has Person mode enabled, a user may not be removed from the Learning admin role even after the corresponding child permission in RBP is removed. SAP says this is expected, not a bug, and occurs when the same person has another active employment that retains the role.

To verify: In Learning Administration > System Administration > Security > Role Management, open an administrator role and check the Users tab.

 

4. RBP change audit reports now come in two versions

You create the reports as before, in Admin Center > Change Audit Reports > Create Configuration Data Report. The Access Reports tab then shows two versions of each report, for example RBP_GROUP_CHANGE_REPORT and RBP_GROUP_CHANGE_REPORT_V2. V2 has additional data fields, broader audit coverage and faster data availability. It is available for four report types:

 

Report

Major enhancements in V2

RBP Group Change Report

For the Group name field, the original captured only updates to existing names. V2 also covers creation and deletion.

RBP Static Group Membership Change Report

Adds a Display Name column showing the user’s display name.

RBP Role Change Report

Splits Permission into three fields: Permission (standard RBP permissions), Advanced Permission (resource-based permissions that require target criteria during setup) and MDF Permission (Metadata Framework permissions).

 

Splits Role Assignment into Role Assignment Basic Details and Advanced Permission Target Criteria. The new Basic Details field covers permission data blocking information.

 

Splits Group into MDF Permission Basic Target Criteria, MDF Permission Basic Data Blocking and MDF Permission Target Criteria for Position.

 

Adds new fields such as Role Description and RBP-Only.

RBP User Role Change Report

Renames RuleId to Role Assignment ID for clearer identification. The Context 4 Key and Context 4 Value columns, unused in the original report, now show the user’s display name.

(Figure 1:  V2 version of RBP reports)

Prerequisite: Change audit logging must be enabled for your system.

Two behaviors to plan for:

1. V2 may contain more data than the original. It is built on a new audit technology that makes data available faster, so when both reports are generated at the same time, V2 may hold more.

(Figure 2: RBP Group Change Report)

(Figure 3: RBP Role Change Report )

 

2. Audit Log Service can return two sets of records per change. If you access RBP change audit data through SAP Audit Log

Service, the payload may contain one set from the new technology and one from the original. Records from the new technology appear sooner, so a query shortly after a change may return only those, and the original records may arrive later. Check the objectType field in the payload to tell them apart. SAP’s Module-Specific Fields, Attribute Names and Coded Values page explains how to identify records from the new technology.

The release note does not say how long both versions will be offered.

Suggested: Make one permission change, generate both reports and keep the comparison as evidence. Tell anyone who consumes Audit Log Service data that each change may appear twice.

 

5. Hide Story report data for forms that never reached a user’s Inbox

A user with Data Access: Story can view Performance Management data in Story reports for all forms matching the selected form templates and target population. That can include forms that never reached their Inbox and are probably irrelevant to them. SAP’s example is Ask for Feedback requests and replies for forms they weren’t involved in.

The new permission Hide Story Report Data for Forms Never in Inbox (User Permissions > Performance) prevents users from seeing that data. It works together with Data Access: Story and is disabled by default. SAP says it helps ensure data privacy and relevance in Performance Management Story reports.

Requirements:

  • Story reports are enabled.
  • Enable Performance Management Access Permission is selected in the Performance Management Feature Settings admin tool.
  • Users are granted Performance > Data Access: Story.

Suggested: Review who holds Data Access: Story and decide whether they should see data for forms that never reached their Inbox. If not, grant the new permission.

 

6. REST API enhancements

  • POST /assignments now returns an id field for the created assignment, so you no longer need a follow-up GET request. Previously it returned only a 201 Created status code.
  • POST /roles and PUT /roles now support an externalCode field for MDF permissions in both requests and responses. For requests involving MDF permissions, you must provide either the MDF entity’s externalCode or its resourceId. The external code applies only to MDF permissions (resource type MDF_OBJECT), not to other resource-based permissions.

SAP will update the API documentation on SAP Business Accelerator Hub (SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permission Management API) on the Valid as Of date, 13 November 2026.

Sample Code 
"resources": [
    {
      "resourceId": 111,
      "externalCode": "obj4qaBEDataSource", //External code of the MDF resource. Only applicable when resourceType is MDF_OBJECT.
      "resourceType": "MDF_OBJECT",
      "selectedActions": [
        {
          "name": "VIEW_HISTORY"
        } ...

Suggested: If you manage roles or assignments through scripts or integrations, check that MDF permission requests supply externalCode or resourceId. You can also use the returned assignment id instead of a follow-up GET.

Proxy can act in that module and its parent. Check the Reporting and Performance Management Forms behavior.

Closing thought

 

Four of these changes tighten control or evidence. Proxy Rights separates managing proxies from being one, the MDF change secures more objects, V2 gives finer audit fields, and the Story permission lets you hide data for forms users never received. The Learning change centralizes administration in RBP, and the API change makes automation easier.

Two changes also act on your roles automatically: the Proxy Rights grant and the Position Management grants. SAP designed them to avoid disruption, so they carry over the access your roles already had. That is our reading, not SAP’s, but it is why both deserve a review before 13 November.

entry.title: SAP Enterprise Service Management Q3 2026 Innovation Highlights
entry.content:
As SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision continues to take shape across our portfolio, in Q3 2026 we delivered powerful new capabilities for SAP Enterprise Service Management (SAP ESM) customers, partners, and practitioners. Whether you are modernizing HR service delivery, managing financial shared services, or looking to drive higher self-service adoption across the enterprise and every business function, the Q3 2026 release has something for you.

Before we dive in, we’re excited to share our customers’ value stories! Take a moment to register for our upcoming webinars and hear about our customers’ deployment journeys and value achieved from unified, AI-led, shared service operations with SAP ESM.

🚀Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Cracking the Code on HR Service Delivery: Enercon's Journey
Featuring Enercon's journey in unifying HR shared service delivery, moderated by HR Tech analyst,  Anita Lettink.
Register here.
 
🚀Thursday, November 19, 2026
Smarter, Faster, Unified: SAP’s Journey to AI-Powered Shared Services
SAP’s global deployment with over 4,000 service professionals live today, serving employees, partners, and customers across 7 business functions.
Register here.

Now, let’s dive into the Q3 2026 innovation highlights including insights on autonomous assistants coming your way!  For even more detailed insights on our Q3 2026 service innovations, register here for the Q3 2026 Release Overview on November 5th, hosted by our product management team.

Intelligent case flow: Less effort with faster resolution

Case management in SAP ESM has proven to deliver the flexibility organizations need to model their shared service processes across the enterprise, coordinating complex workflows between automation and human action. The Q3 2026 enhancements to Case Flow reduce manual steps for both service representatives and administrators, allowing structured service processes to progress more naturally and more efficiently without unnecessary intervention.

Auto Complete Conditions for Input Steps in Case Flow

Input steps within a case flow allow service representatives to capture or update structured data in context without navigating away from the case. Until now, however, marking an input step as complete was always a manual action, even when the required conditions were clearly satisfied.

With this Q3 2026 release, administrators can now define conditions under which an input step will automatically mark itself as complete. When those conditions are met, for example, when specific field values have been set or when a case reaches a particular status, the system evaluates the configured logic and completes the step without requiring a service representative to take action.

Why it matters:

  • High-volume, structured processes benefit most. Think onboarding workflows, procurement inquiries, or HR case handling where multiple input steps follow predictable completion patterns.
  • Service representatives can focus on the steps that genuinely require their judgment, rather than clicking through steps the system can already identify as complete.
  • Administrators retain full control over when auto-completion applies, using the same familiar condition builder available throughout the Case Designer.

Auto Trigger for Case Approval Step

Approval steps in SAP ESM case flows are a critical governance mechanism, ensuring that key decisions are reviewed by the right people before a case proceeds. However, a common source of delay in approval-heavy workflows is simply that service representatives forget, or are too busy, to manually submit the approval request.

This enhancement allows administrators to configure an approval step to auto-submit as soon as its preconditions are met. Once the case reaches the configured state and all entry conditions are satisfied, the approval request is triggered automatically, without service representative intervention.

Why it matters:

  • Eliminates a common bottleneck in approval-gated workflows, particularly in financial shared services and compliance-driven processes where timely approvals are essential.
  • Works alongside existing precondition configuration, giving administrators precise control over when auto-submission is appropriate.
  • Approvers still receive requests and must act. This feature automates the submission, not the decision itself.

Accelerate Financial Service Delivery with Contract Accounts

For organizations delivering financial shared services, whether handling billing inquiries, payment disputes, collection workloads, or contract account management, having complete financial context within the service case is not a nice-to-have; it is essential. The Q3 2026 release introduces a deeply integrated Contract Account View, connecting SAP ESM directly to SAP Cloud ERP FI-CA financial data and bringing it into the agent's hands without the need to switch systems.

Contract Account View: Financial Documents, Invoices, Payments, and Collections

Service representatives working on financial inquiries can now see a complete picture of the customer's financial position right from the ESM agent desktop, without navigating to SAP Cloud ERP transaction screens. These include:

  • Financial Documents and Open Items: All FI-CA transactions for the past 365 days (configurable) are displayed, aggregated by document number.
  • Invoices: The last 12 months of invoices, billing documents, and billing plans are available, each with a direct link to the PDF printout.
  • Payments: All payment documents posted in the last 365 days are visible with real-time, color-coded status tags.
  • Collections: The full collections history from SAP Cloud ERP FI-CA is surfaced directly in ESM, covering dunning records, returns, and write-offs.

Contract Account View: Payment Arrangements, Locks, and Correspondence

Beyond raw financial data, the Contract Account View also provides service representatives with the context needed to understand active agreements, account restrictions, and prior correspondence, all without leaving the service agent desktop.

  • Payment Arrangements: All Promise to Pay agreements and Installment Plans for the contract account are visible in either card or table format.
  • Locks: Active and expired locks applied to the contract account are displayed, including lock type, reason, and date range.
  • Correspondences and Bank Data: Complete correspondence history, key attributes, and bank data, are available in a dedicated tab.

This provides service representatives with a comprehensive financial picture in one place.

Elevating the self-service experience

The self-service application is how employees experience enterprise service management directly. Two Q3 2026 enhancements give administrators more precise control over what employees see and how they interact with their cases, resulting in a cleaner, more focused experience and fewer unnecessary support contacts.

Controlled Case Visibility in List View

In organizations where SAP ESM supports multiple lines of business, not every case type is intended for employee self-service visibility. With this Q3 2026 update, a new attribute has been added to the case type configuration to specify self-service relevance. Only cases belonging to case types that have been marked as self-service relevant in Case Type Configuration will appear in the employee's list. Cases associated with internal, service representative-only, or back-office case types will not be visible in the self-service interface.

Why it matters:

  • Employees see only the cases that are relevant and actionable for them, reducing confusion and erroneous selection.
  • Administrators gain precise control over the self-service experience, aligning what employees see with the organization's service delivery model.
  • This is particularly valuable for organizations running ESM across multiple functions such as HR, Finance, IT, and Procurement, where different case types serve very different audiences.

Enhanced Case Communication History

Understanding the full history of a case, including who said what, when, and through which channel, is fundamental to the self-service experience. Before this release, timeline events and case conversations were combined in a single Conversations tab, which made it harder to quickly locate a particular event or communication.

This enhancement restructures how case history is presented in the self-service interface, making it easier to locate specific events and communications, reducing inquiries back to the service representative and improving resolution times.

Why it matters:

  • A dedicated Timeline tab now presents all case events in chronological order, including status changes, assignments, workflow transitions, and other system-level activities, giving employees a clear audit trail of everything that has happened on their case.
  • The Conversations tab has been refined to focus on actual communications. A new Past Conversations section surfaces all non-internal notes, providing employees with a clear record of the dialogue between them and the service team.
  • Internal notes intended only for service representatives remain hidden from the employee-facing view, ensuring operational transparency is maintained without exposing confidential service team communications.

Preview: Autonomous Assistants

One of the most exciting themes at SAP SAPPHIRE and SAP Connect was the emergence of autonomous, AI-led assistants within SAP ESM. These are not incremental improvements to existing features; they represent a fundamentally different way of working, where Joule Work takes on complex, multi-step service and finance tasks with contextual intelligence and minimal human intervention. We are pleased to share an early look at two assistants currently progressing through Early Adopter Care, with general availability coming soon.

Recurring Receivables Assistant

Managing recurring revenue operations at scale is complex. Collections specialists, invoicing teams, subscription managers, and accounts receivable clerks each work within their own slice of a highly interconnected process, and when an exception occurs, resolving it typically requires manual coordination across multiple systems and stakeholders.

The Recurring Receivables Assistant coordinates execution across subscription orders and contracts, invoices, disputes, payments, and collections. The assistant helps teams prioritize collections, manage subscription contract changes, correct invoices, and resolve customer disputes and payment exceptions across multiple applications and solutions with clearer issue context and faster customer communication.

The assistant supports the core business stages across the receivables lifecycle:

  • Prioritize: Surfaces high-impact accounts, explains risk drivers, and recommends the next-best collection action, so collections specialists focus effort where it matters most.
  • Prevent: Detects invoice rejection risk before downstream impact occurs, identifies likely root causes, and recommends corrections, reducing exceptions before they slow collections.
  • Correct: Identifies contract data issues, validates corrections, simulates billing impact, and guides subscription specialists through the update, unblocking invoice and payment flow.
  • Resolve: Investigates payment exceptions and unmatched payments, connects invoice and contract context, and guides AR clerks through resolution, closing issues with less manual investigation.

Case Management Assistant

Every service representative manages cases, but the experience of working through a complex, multi-step case, coordinating with customers, extracting information from attachments, triggering backend processes, and knowing what to do next, can still be demanding and time-consuming. The Case Management Assistant is designed to change that.

Available as a standalone starting point for a service interaction or embedded directly in the SAP ESM agent desktop, the Case Management Assistant is a Joule-powered AI agent that works alongside service representatives throughout the full case lifecycle. 

Key dimensions of the assistant's capability include:

  • Contextual guidance: The assistant understands where a case is in its workflow and surfaces relevant next steps, so service representatives spend less time figuring out what to do and more time doing it.
  • Document and entity extraction: Attachments, emails, and case descriptions are automatically analyzed to extract key information, reducing manual data entry and improving case accuracy from the outset.
  • Communication assistance: Service representatives receive assistance drafting and refining customer communications within the case, ensuring timely and consistent responses that reflect the service organization's standards.
  • Connected process execution: The assistant can trigger actions in connected SAP systems, such as SAP Cloud ERP, directly from the case context, without requiring service representatives to navigate to separate applications.

Early adopter customers are actively engaged, already reporting measurable reductions in service representative effort. Stay tuned for the general availability announcement, coming soon.

Additional Information

For additional Q3 2026 innovations relevant for SAP Enterprise Service Management, register for the upcoming Q3 2026 Release Webinar. To stay up-to-date as we release capabilities each month and to get a full view of what’s new for Q3 2026, reference the What’s New page in our help portal. Also, reference these valuable links for more on SAP ESM and SAP CX solutions:

SAP ESM’s free trial: Get hands-on experience today with an HR service delivery scenario (Finance shared services coming in November 2026).

SAP Learning ESM Course

SAP Release Navigator

SAP Service Cloud V2 Certification Course

And finally, thank you. The continued growth of this community and the willingness of its members to share, question, and collaborate are what move SAP ESM forward. Every SAP employee, partner, and customer benefits from the collective knowledge exchanged here, and it is genuinely appreciated.

The SAP ESM community is the best place to ask questions, share experiences, and stay current on what's coming. Use the SAP Enterprise Service Management managed tag when posting on SAP ESM topics in the community.

Thank you for being part of this community! We value your participation and look forward to continuing the conversation.

entry.title: Calling SAP SuccessFactors from Postman with OAuth 2.0 (SAML Bearer Assertion) - No External Tools
entry.content:
SAP SuccessFactors is retiring HTTP Basic Authentication (user and password) for its APIs. The retirement is planned for November 2026, and published sources give either 13 or 20 November, so the earlier date is the safer one to plan for. After that date, OData calls and SOAP calls such as CompoundEmployee will only accept token-based authentication.

If you use SAP Integration Suite (CPI), the switch is mostly a matter of configuration: you create an OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion credential and the adapter handles the rest. Manual testing in Postman has no equivalent built-in support. This post explains how to reproduce, step by step, what CPI does internally, using only Postman and OpenSSL.

The complete Postman collection, with all scripts in English, is attached to this post.

What you will be able to do

  • Generate your own RSA key pair and X.509 certificate.
  • Register an OAuth 2.0 client application in SAP SuccessFactors.
  • Build and digitally sign a SAML 2.0 assertion inside Postman, without any external tool.
  • Exchange the assertion for an OAuth access token and call the OData API.
  • Open an SFAPI session with the token and query CompoundEmployee over SOAP.

No prior OAuth or SAML knowledge is assumed. The explanations cover what happens at each step and why.

How it works

The method is the OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion grant. Instead of sending a password, you send SuccessFactors a short XML document, the assertion. The assertion states that the application with a given API Key is acting as a given user and that the request is valid for the next 10 minutes. You sign the assertion with a private key. SuccessFactors verifies the signature with the public certificate you registered earlier. If the signature matches, it returns an access token valid for about 24 hours, and you attach that token to every API call.

The setup has two parts:

  1. One-time setup: create a technical user with the right permissions, generate a key pair, register the certificate in an OAuth client in SuccessFactors, and create a Postman environment.
  2. Every session: generate the assertion, get the token, then call the OData API or open an SFAPI session and query CompoundEmployee.

Step A: Technical user and permissions

Create or reuse a dedicated technical user, for example API_TECH_USER, and assign a permission role that includes:

  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS OData API and Foundation OData API, for access to Employee Central entities.
  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS SOAP API, required for CompoundEmployee.
  • General User Permission → SFAPI User Login, required to open an SFAPI session.
  • The target population and field-level RBP. These define which employees and fields the API returns. If they are too narrow, you get empty results.

The permission Allow Admin to Access OData API through Basic Authentication is not needed for OAuth. Once the migration is complete, you can remove it to verify that nothing still depends on Basic Authentication.

Step B: Key pair and certificate

Generate a self-signed certificate and private key with OpenSSL:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -sha256 -days 36500 -nodes \
  -keyout private.pem -out cert.pem -subj "/CN=postman-sf-ACMECORPT1"

Key points:

  • -nodes leaves the private key unencrypted. The Postman script needs an unencrypted PKCS#8 key.
  • The validity period is a decision to make together with the customer, in line with their security policy. A long validity avoids renewing the certificate and updating every Postman environment each year. A shorter lifetime reduces the impact if the key leaks. Either way, record the expiry date with openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -enddate.

SuccessFactors and the Postman variables need the Base64 content without the BEGIN/END lines and without line breaks. On Linux, macOS or Git Bash:

grep -v -- "-----" private.pem | tr -d '\n' > private_b64.txt
grep -v -- "-----" cert.pem    | tr -d '\n' > cert_b64.txt

On Windows PowerShell, use the equivalent Get-Content, Where-Object and Set-Content commands. The public certificate goes to SuccessFactors and to the Postman variable certificate_b64. The private key goes only into the Postman variable private_key_b64, and it must never be shared.

Step C: Register the OAuth client in SuccessFactors

In Admin Center, open Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and choose Register Client Application. Fill in:

  • Company: the tenant company ID (prefilled).
  • Application Name: free text. It appears in the token as issuedFor.
  • Application URL: used for identification only. No call is made to it.
  • Bind to Users: checked, and the technical user ID added. This restricts token issuance to the listed users and is recommended.
  • X.509 Certificate: paste the single-line Base64 certificate.

Do not click Generate X.509 Certificate. That creates a different key pair, and you already have yours. After registering, open the client and copy the API Key. It becomes the Postman variable client_id. The API Key is not a secret on its own, but it cannot be used to obtain tokens without the private key.

Step Postman environment

Create an environment, for example SF ACME Preview, with these variables:

Variable Content

urlThe API server of your data center, without a trailing slash. This is not the UI URL. Find it in SAP's list of SuccessFactors API servers.
userThe technical user ID from Step A. It goes into the assertion NameID.
companyThe tenant company ID.
client_idThe API Key of the OAuth client.
private_key_b64Content of private_b64.txt. Set the type to secret and fill only the Current value.
certificate_b64Content of cert_b64.txt. Optional, added to the assertion KeyInfo.
assertion, assertion_xml, sf_token, sf_token_exp, sessionIdLeft empty. They are written by the requests.

Postman keeps an Initial value and a Current value for each variable. Keep the private key, tokens and assertions in the Current value only, so they are not synced to the workspace or included in exports.

Collection structure

The collection can be run from top to bottom with the Collection Runner, or one request at a time:

  • SF SAML Bearer step by step
    1. Generate assertion: downloads the jsrsasign library and builds the signed assertion.
    2. Get token: exchanges the assertion for an access token.
    3. Call OData resource: calls the OData API with the Bearer token.
  • CompoundEmployee
    • Login CE: opens the SFAPI session.
    • GET CompoundEmployee: runs the SOAP query.
  • AllInOneCall (optional): a pre-request script that obtains a token automatically when needed.

Request 1: Generating the SAML assertion

SuccessFactors does not create the assertion for you. The old /oauth/idp endpoint is deprecated, because it required sending the private key over the network. So the assertion has to be built and signed on the client side. Postman's sandbox includes CryptoJS for hashing but no RSA signing, so the script first downloads jsrsasign, a pure JavaScript cryptography library.

The assertion contains:

  • ID and IssueInstant: a random identifier and the current UTC time.
  • Issuer: the fixed value www.successfactors.com.
  • Signature: an enveloped XML signature, placed right after the Issuer.
  • Subject / NameID: the technical user the API calls will run as.
  • SubjectConfirmationData: the Recipient is the /oauth/token endpoint.
  • Conditions: a validity window from 5 minutes in the past to 10 minutes in the future.
  • AttributeStatement: an api_key attribute with the client ID, which tells SuccessFactors which registered certificate to use.

The signature is produced in three steps. First, the assertion without the signature is hashed with SHA-256. Second, a small SignedInfo block describing the algorithms and the digest is assembled. Third, SignedInfo is signed with the private key using RSA-SHA256. SuccessFactors repeats the same computation with the registered certificate. If one byte differs, the verification fails.

One detail matters a lot: XML signatures are computed over a canonical form of the XML (Exclusive XML Canonicalization, exc-c14n). Postman has no canonicalization library, so the script writes the XML already in canonical form, with no spaces or line breaks between elements, attributes in alphabetical order and explicit closing tags. Do not reformat or indent the XML parts of the script. A single extra space breaks the signature.

Request 2: Getting the access token

The assertion is exchanged at {{url}}/oauth/token as an x-www-form-urlencoded body with four fields: client_id, company_id, grant_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer, and assertion. This must happen within the 10-minute window of the assertion.

The post-response script stores sf_token and an expiry timestamp. The expiry is set 5 minutes early to avoid using a token that expires in the middle of a call.

The token is Base64-encoded JSON. Decoding it is a useful sanity check, because it shows which API key and which user it was issued for.

Request 3: Calling the OData API

With the token, OData calls are simple: the token goes in the Authorization: Bearer header. For example:

  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/User?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/PerPerson?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/EmpJob?$filter=userId eq '100001'&$select=userId,startDate,company,department,jobCode&$format=json

To check whether a token is still valid, call {{url}}/oauth/validate with the Bearer token.

CompoundEmployee via SFAPI

CompoundEmployee is exposed by the SFAPI, the older SOAP API. Unlike OData, SFAPI works with sessions. A login operation returns a session ID, which is also set as the JSESSIONID cookie, and every query must carry that session.

The key finding from testing: sending the Bearer token directly on the query returns INVALID_SESSION. The token must first be used in a login call, and the login body must have empty companyId, username and password elements. If companyId or username are filled in, SuccessFactors attempts a classic password login and fails with FAILED_AUTHENTICATION. If the password element is removed altogether, the request fails schema validation. So the working combination is empty elements plus the Bearer header, which returns a session ID.

Then, for the query:

  • Set the cookie explicitly: Cookie: JSESSIONID={{sessionId}}.
  • Disable the Postman cookie jar, so that old session cookies are not sent.
  • Use a SOAP query with a SELECT on CompoundEmployee, for example on person, personal_information, employment_information and job_information.
  • For incremental extracts, add a delta filter such as WHERE last_modified_on > to_datetime('...'). Inside XML, the greater-than sign must be written as >.
  • When the response contains <hasMore>true</hasMore>, call queryMore with the returned querySessionId until hasMore is false.

The SFAPI session expires after 10 minutes of inactivity. If you get INVALID_SESSION, run the login again.

Lifetimes and run order

Item Lifetime When to regenerate

SAML assertion10 minutesRun Request 1 again if Request 2 is sent later than that.
Access tokenAbout 24 hoursRun Requests 1 and 2 again. The step-by-step flow does not refresh automatically.
SFAPI session10 minutes of inactivityRun Login CE again on INVALID_SESSION.
CertificateAs generated, or as agreed with the customerRotate before expiry: new key pair, then update the OAuth client and the Postman variables together.

A typical session is: generate the assertion, get the token, call OData as needed, log in to SFAPI, then run the CompoundEmployee query.

Troubleshooting

A few of the errors encountered while building this setup:

  • Identifier 't' has already been declared: the library was loaded in the same scope as the script. Load it with new Function(...), as the script does.
  • getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND undefined: a variable does not exist in the selected environment. Check the variable names and that the environment is selected.
  • Error from KEYUTIL.getKey: the key is not PKCS#8 or it is truncated. Regenerate it with -nodes, and check that the first line is -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.
  • /oauth/token rejects the assertion: the certificate registered in SuccessFactors does not match the key, the XML was altered, the clocks are out of sync, or the assertion is older than 10 minutes.
  • INVALID_SESSION on SOAP calls: the query was sent with the Bearer token instead of the session cookie, or an old cookie was sent. Log in first and disable the cookie jar.
  • FAILED_AUTHENTICATION on login: the credential elements were not empty, or the Bearer header was not set on the request.

Security

  • The private key is equivalent to the credentials of the technical user. Keep it only in the Postman Current value, marked as secret. Never commit it to a repository or share it in chats. Ideally, each colleague generates their own key pair and OAuth client.
  • Never send tokens to third-party hosts. The request that downloads the library from cdnjs must use No Auth. An inherited Bearer token would be sent to that host.
  • Use a dedicated technical user with minimal permissions and a restricted target population, and enable Bind to Users on the OAuth client.
  • Use separate key pairs and OAuth clients for each tenant, for example preview and production.
  • Once OAuth works, remove the Basic Authentication permission from the technical user.

Attached material

The attached Postman collection, OAuth Assertion - SuccessFactors, contains all the requests described above, in the order they should run, the complete Request 1 script, and the optional AllInOneCall request, which handles token renewal automatically.

Note: SAP Community does not accept .json attachments, so the collection is provided as a .txt file. Rename it to OAuth_Assertion_SuccessFactors.postman_collection.json before importing it into Postman. The file content is unchanged.

Before importing it, create the environment described in Step D. The collection contains no secrets. All tenant data in the examples (URLs, company ID, user, API key, keys and IDs) are fictitious, so replace them with your own tenant values.

I hope this helps anyone who needs to test SuccessFactors APIs from Postman without Basic Authentication. Questions and feedback are welcome in the comments

entry.title: How to Enable SAP Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Using SAP BTP and Cloud Identity Services
entry.content:
1. Understanding the Architecture

For a SuccessFactors implementation, the Joule landscape can be viewed in three layers.

Experience Layer

The user works primarily in SAP SuccessFactors.

Joule is embedded into the SuccessFactors user experience. Users don't need to leave SuccessFactors simply to interact with Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

Conceptually:

Employee / Manager → SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule

AI and Platform Layer

Although Joule appears inside SuccessFactors, Joule itself runs as a service on SAP BTP. [https://le...essfactors]

SAP SuccessFactors continues to own the HR business data and processes, while Joule provides the conversational and orchestration layer.

Conceptually:

SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule → SAP BTP

Identity and Authorization Layer

The third area is identity and authorization.

SAP Cloud Identity Services forms part of the Joule identity architecture, while SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions determine which SuccessFactors information and functionality a user is authorized to access. [https://le...essfactors]

This separation is important. Enabling Joule does not give the user unrestricted access to SuccessFactors.

2. Check the Prerequisites

Before configuring anything, start by validating that your landscape satisfies SAP's Joule prerequisites.

SAP's Setting Up Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Learning content lists prerequisites including:

  • SAP BTP account with the required Joule entitlement
  • Joule entitlement identified as das-application
  • SAP SuccessFactors license
  • Joule availability for the applicable data center
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants
  • SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start [https://le...essfactors]

The last prerequisite is worth noting.

Your users may access Joule directly from the SuccessFactors experience and may not use a separate SAP Build Work Zone site as their business launchpad. Nevertheless, SAP's current Learning material lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start among the prerequisites for the overall Joule setup. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, don't interpret "using SuccessFactors as the launchpad" as meaning that all SAP Start / Build Work Zone platform dependencies can simply be omitted.

Follow the dependencies presented by the Joule onboarding process for your particular landscape.

3. Check the Required Administrator Access

Before starting the implementation, make sure the configuration team has the required administrative access.

SAP's SuccessFactors Joule setup guidance identifies the following administrative roles:

  • SAP SuccessFactors Administrator
  • SAP BTP Global Account Administrator
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Administrator [https://he...cale=en-US]

This is important because the onboarding isn't limited to SuccessFactors configuration. It crosses the SuccessFactors, BTP and identity landscapes.

At this stage, your initial checklist should therefore be:

  • SuccessFactors tenant and license are available
  • SAP BTP Global Account is identified
  • Joule entitlement is available
  • Appropriate SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants are available
  • Required administrators have access
  • Joule availability for the relevant landscape/data center has been checked
  • SAP Start / Build Work Zone requirement has been assessed according to the current Joule onboarding model

4. Verify the Joule Entitlement in SAP BTP

The next step is to verify that the SAP BTP Global Account has the required Joule entitlement.

SAP Learning specifically identifies the Joule entitlement as:

das-application

SAP recommends checking the entitlements available in the BTP Global Account. [https://le...essfactors]

If you have the appropriate SuccessFactors license but the Joule entitlement isn't available, SAP Learning advises contacting your SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Don't try to compensate for a missing Joule entitlement by manually creating unrelated BTP services. Resolve the commercial/provisioning issue first.

A successful implementation starts with the correct entitlement being delivered to the correct SAP BTP Global Account.

5. Prepare SAP Cloud Identity Services

Once the commercial and BTP prerequisites are established, the next major area is identity.

SAP Learning explicitly lists SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants as a prerequisite for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

Before starting Joule onboarding, document the participating systems and identity landscape.

At minimum, identify:

  • SAP SuccessFactors tenant
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant
  • SAP BTP Global Account
  • Relevant BTP landscape
  • Production versus non-production systems
  • User identities used across the participating systems

This might seem administrative, but it becomes extremely useful when troubleshooting authentication and user provisioning.

A common source of confusion is treating IAS and IPS as though they perform the same function. They should be considered separately.

6. Understand IAS: Identity Authentication

SAP Identity Authentication is part of SAP Cloud Identity Services.

From an implementation perspective, think about Identity Authentication as the authentication side of the architecture.

The central question is:

How is the identity of the user established across the participating SAP applications?

Your Joule implementation therefore needs to consider how SuccessFactors, Joule/BTP and SAP Cloud Identity Services participate in establishing a consistent user identity.

SAP's Learning material identifies active SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants as part of the prerequisites for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

The exact configuration should follow the Joule onboarding guidance appropriate to your tenant rather than assuming a generic IAS configuration will be sufficient.

7. Understand IPS: Identity Provisioning

Authentication isn't the whole identity story.

The second area is Identity Provisioning Service (IPS).

Conceptually:

IAS answers the authentication/identity question.

IPS deals with provisioning identities between the relevant systems.

SAP's Joule provisioning documentation explicitly includes Configure Identity Provisioning Service within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Therefore, don't document your implementation simply as "IAS configured."

Your architecture documentation should separately record:

Authentication

How users authenticate and how their identities are established across the participating applications.

Provisioning

How identities required by the Joule landscape are provisioned and synchronized.

The actual source, target and provisioning configuration should follow the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the landscape being implemented.

8. Start the Official Joule Onboarding Process

Once the prerequisites, BTP entitlement and Cloud Identity Services landscape are ready, proceed with Joule onboarding.

This is an area where it is especially important not to follow an outdated blog containing a static list of destinations, service instances or role collections.

SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation directs administrators to:

Follow the Joule Onboarding Guide to finish the setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

SAP Learning also points to SAP's activation guidance for implementing Joule with SuccessFactors. [https://le...essfactors]

Use the official onboarding process applicable to your system.

During this phase, validate that you are working with:

  • The intended BTP Global Account
  • The intended SuccessFactors system
  • The correct SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape
  • The required Joule entitlement
  • The appropriate production or non-production environment

Avoid manually reproducing configuration from an old implementation unless that configuration is still explicitly required by the current onboarding process.

9. Understand the Role of SAP Build Work Zone / SAP Start

This particular topic can create confusion for SuccessFactors customers.

In this implementation scenario, the end user experiences Joule through SAP SuccessFactors.

That does not mean you should automatically remove SAP Build Work Zone/SAP Start from the technical architecture.

SAP's current Learning material for setting up Joule with SuccessFactors explicitly lists:

SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start

among the prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

The accurate way to describe the architecture is therefore:

SuccessFactors is the user-facing business application from which users interact with Joule. The technical services and platform dependencies required by SAP's current Joule onboarding model are provisioned separately according to SAP's onboarding guidance.

This is particularly important if you're coming from an S/4HANA Cloud background.

Don't equate the user's launchpad with every underlying platform component used to deliver Joule.

10. Complete the SuccessFactors-Side Joule Setup

After completing the required Joule onboarding activities, move to the SuccessFactors-side configuration.

The critical concept here is that provisioning Joule doesn't automatically give every SuccessFactors user access to it.

You still need to control which users have permission to use Joule.

SAP's SuccessFactors documentation explicitly identifies an Access to Joule permission. [https://he...cale=en-US]

In SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions, the documented permission is located under:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Assign this permission through the appropriate SuccessFactors RBP roles according to the users who should have access to Joule.

This gives you a clear separation:

Technical onboarding enables the Joule service.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions control which SuccessFactors users can access Joule.

11. Existing SuccessFactors Authorizations Still Apply

Granting Access to Joule should not be confused with granting unrestricted access to SuccessFactors functionality.

SAP states that the business data and actions accessed through Joule continue to be governed by existing SuccessFactors authorizations. [https://le...essfactors]

This means two conditions need to be considered.

Condition 1: Joule access

Is the user authorized to access Joule?

Condition 2: Business authorization

Is the same user authorized in SuccessFactors to access the requested HR information or execute the requested business operation?

Both are important.

For example, enabling Joule for an employee should not be considered a mechanism for bypassing Role-Based Permissions protecting manager or HR information.

This is one of the most important design principles to explain to your security and HR authorization teams.

12. Configure Employee Central Quick Actions Where Applicable

If you're using SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central, there is another configuration area to review.

SAP recommends enabling Employee Central Quick Actions and configuring the corresponding templates for Employee Central customers using Joule. [https://he...cale=en-US]

The reason this is relevant is that Joule isn't purely a question-and-answer interface.

SAP's architecture description discusses Joule supporting conversational interaction involving navigation and transactional interactions in the business application. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, for Employee Central implementations, review the Quick Actions needed for the supported Joule use cases you intend to make available.

Don't assume that every Employee Central action automatically becomes available through Joule.

Always validate the particular use case against the current SuccessFactors Joule documentation.

13. Validate Joule in SAP SuccessFactors

Once the onboarding, identity configuration and SuccessFactors authorization settings are complete, validate the solution from the SuccessFactors experience.

Use a test user that has:

  • Access to Joule
  • Correct identity configuration
  • Appropriate SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Access to the underlying SuccessFactors functionality being tested

The first validation is simple:

Can the user access Joule from the SuccessFactors user experience?

If yes, don't stop there.

The next validation is:

Can Joule access only the SuccessFactors information and operations that this user is authorized to use?

SAP states that existing SuccessFactors authorizations govern the data and actions available through Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

That means functional and security validation should be performed together.

14. Test Different Authorization Scenarios

A good implementation should test more than one type of user.

Employee User

Use an employee account with normal Employee Self-Service permissions.

Validate the supported Joule scenarios applicable to employees.

Manager User

Use a manager account with appropriate manager permissions.

Validate supported manager scenarios where applicable.

Restricted User

Use an account intentionally lacking access to selected SuccessFactors information or functionality.

Validate that giving the user access to Joule doesn't extend the user's access beyond the underlying SuccessFactors authorization.

The purpose is not merely to prove that Joule opens successfully.

The purpose is to prove:

Joule availability + correct identity + correct SuccessFactors authorization + supported use case

work together.

15. Understand Which SuccessFactors Use Cases Are Supported

Another important implementation step is determining what you actually want users to do with Joule.

Not every SuccessFactors capability should be assumed to have a corresponding Joule capability.

SAP maintains documentation for the supported Joule capabilities and use cases within SuccessFactors. [https://he...essfactors]

For example, SAP's SuccessFactors Onboarding documentation lists scenarios such as:

  • Completing required onboarding tasks
  • Assigning a buddy
  • Viewing pending offboarding tasks
  • Directing new hires to their Onboarding Checklist and Onboarding Guide [https://he...cale=en-US]

This demonstrates why the business configuration underneath Joule remains important.

Having the Joule window available doesn't automatically make every HR operation available conversationally.

For any implementation, create a list of the specific SuccessFactors Joule use cases that your organization plans to enable and validate each against current SAP documentation.

16. End-to-End Implementation Sequence

Putting everything together, the recommended implementation flow is:

Step 1: Verify SuccessFactors prerequisites

Confirm the SuccessFactors licensing and applicable Joule prerequisites.

Step 2: Verify Joule availability

Check whether Joule is available for the applicable SuccessFactors landscape/data center according to the current SAP guidance. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 3: Verify the BTP Global Account

Confirm that you're working with the intended SAP BTP Global Account.

Step 4: Verify Joule entitlement

Check that the Joule das-application entitlement is available in the BTP landscape. [https://le...essfactors]

If the entitlement is missing for an appropriately licensed scenario, follow SAP's guidance and contact the SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 5: Establish the SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape

Identify the SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant participating in the implementation. SAP lists active Cloud Identity Services tenants among the SuccessFactors Joule prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 6: Address authentication

Follow the Joule onboarding guidance for the required Identity Authentication configuration.

Step 7: Address identity provisioning

Configure the required Identity Provisioning integration according to the current onboarding flow. SAP's Joule provisioning documentation includes Identity Provisioning configuration within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 8: Complete Joule onboarding

Follow the official Joule Onboarding Guide, as directed by SAP's SuccessFactors documentation. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 9: Handle SAP Start / Build Work Zone dependencies

Implement the applicable platform dependency according to the Joule onboarding model. SAP's current Learning content lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start as a prerequisite. [https://le...essfactors]

This doesn't mean users must use a separate Work Zone site as their SuccessFactors launchpad.

Step 10: Configure SuccessFactors Joule access

Grant the relevant SuccessFactors users:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 11: Review SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions

Ensure users have the underlying SuccessFactors authorization required by each business use case. Joule continues to operate within these authorization boundaries. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 12: Configure Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

For Employee Central scenarios, review and configure the Quick Actions recommended by SAP. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 13: Validate Joule

Test Joule from the SAP SuccessFactors user experience.

Step 14: Validate business use cases

Test the actual supported employee and manager use cases required by your organization.

Step 15: Validate authorization boundaries

Confirm that Joule respects the underlying SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

17. Troubleshooting Approach

If Joule isn't working after configuration, troubleshoot the solution layer by layer instead of changing multiple components simultaneously.

Joule isn't available at all

First verify:

  • Joule entitlement
  • BTP landscape
  • Joule onboarding completion
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

User can't access Joule

Verify:

  • User identity
  • Relevant Cloud Identity Services configuration
  • Identity provisioning
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

Joule opens but a business request doesn't work

Verify:

  • Whether that particular Joule use case is supported
  • User's SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Required SuccessFactors business configuration
  • Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

This layer-by-layer troubleshooting method is my recommended implementation approach. The individual requirements above should still be validated against the current SAP onboarding documentation.

18. Final Implementation Checklist

Before declaring the solution ready, validate the following.

Licensing and Landscape

  • SuccessFactors license verified
  • Joule availability verified
  • Correct BTP Global Account identified
  • Correct landscape selected
  • Joule das-application entitlement available

Identity

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services available
  • Authentication requirements completed according to Joule onboarding
  • Identity provisioning requirements completed
  • User identity is consistent across the participating landscape

Joule

  • Official Joule onboarding completed
  • Required platform services provisioned
  • SuccessFactors integration completed

SuccessFactors

  • Access to Joule permission assigned
  • Target users correctly included in RBP roles
  • Underlying SuccessFactors permissions validated
  • Employee Central Quick Actions configured where applicable

Validation

  • Joule accessible from SuccessFactors
  • Employee scenario validated
  • Manager scenario validated where applicable
  • Restricted-user scenario validated
  • RBP authorization boundaries confirmed
  • Required SuccessFactors Joule use cases tested

Conclusion

The most important point when implementing Joule for SAP SuccessFactors is understanding that this isn't simply a switch inside SuccessFactors.

The implementation spans multiple layers:

SAP SuccessFactors provides the HR business application and remains the system of record.

SAP Joule on SAP BTP provides the conversational AI and orchestration experience.

SAP Cloud Identity Services participates in the identity architecture.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions continue to control access to HR data and business functionality. [https://le...essfactors]

For users, however, the experience can remain straightforward: they interact with Joule from SAP SuccessFactors while the underlying BTP and identity landscape provides the services required to enable that experience.

For implementation teams, the safest sequence is therefore:

Prerequisites → Entitlement → Identity → Provisioning → Joule Onboarding → SuccessFactors Permissions → Quick Actions → Business Use Cases → Security Validation

Most importantly, always use the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the tenant being implemented instead of relying exclusively on older manual configuration procedures. SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation explicitly directs administrators to the Joule Onboarding Guide for setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Official SAP References

SAP Help documentation covering Joule capabilities, assistants, agents and individual SuccessFactors use cases. [https://he...essfactors]

SAP Help setup guidance covering administrator prerequisites, the Joule Onboarding Guide, Access to Joule permission and Employee Central Quick Actions. [https://he...cale=en-US]

SAP Help documentation covering customer-managed provisioning and the Identity Provisioning configuration associated with SuccessFactors integration. [https://he...cale=en-US]
